al_unshackled.blurb: Unshackled is one of the sandstone walls lining the rim road of Little River Canyon National Preserve, in the northeast corner of the state. All 28 climbs here are bolted sport lines, and the grading skews hard: a handful of 5.10s and one 5.9, then a strong middle in the 5.11s and 5.12s, with the bulk of the wall at 5.13 and one line a notch higher. The rock is good sandstone and the climbing is steep and physical rather than gentle. It suits strong sport climbers, not beginners. No camping in the preserve.
al_unshackled.parking_note: Park only in the designated roadside pulloffs along the canyon rim road (Highway 176), with all tires clear of the pavement. The preserve is open sunrise to sunset.

al_jungle_gym_grey_wall.blurb: Jungle Gym and Grey Wall share a stretch of sandstone cliff beside the rim road in Little River Canyon National Preserve, near Fort Payne. The 27 routes are all bolted sport climbs, and they cluster tightly: a single 5.10, a few 5.11s, and a big majority at 5.12, with a small number of 5.13s. That makes it a good place for climbers who are already comfortable leading in the low-to-mid 5.12 range and want a day of steep, sustained pulling on solid sandstone. There is little here for newcomers. Use the roadside pulloffs, stay out of the roadway, and do not add or remove any bolts. Camping is not permitted in the preserve.
al_jungle_gym_grey_wall.parking_note: Park only in the designated roadside pulloffs along the canyon rim road (Highway 176), with all tires clear of the pavement. The preserve is open sunrise to sunset.

al_concave_the.blurb: The Concave is a steep sandstone wall in Little River Canyon National Preserve, reached from a pulloff on the canyon rim road. Almost everything here is bolted sport climbing, with a lone trad line and one easy outlier. The rest starts around 5.11, then builds toward a heavy concentration of 5.13 climbs and a few 5.14s, which is why it is known as a destination for strong, powerful sport climbers. The rock is quality sandstone and the angle is demanding. Beginners and anyone below the low 5.11s will find little to climb. Respect the preserve rules: no adding or removing bolts, no camping, and leashed dogs only.
al_concave_the.parking_note: Park only in the designated roadside pulloffs along the canyon rim road (Highway 176), with all tires clear of the pavement. The preserve is open sunrise to sunset.

al_turtle_rock.blurb: Turtle Rock is one section of Sand Rock, also called Cherokee Rock Village, a county-run park above Weiss Lake near Leesburg and Centre. It mixes about a dozen bolted sport lines with ten trad routes on sandstone. Grades run from the 5.7 and 5.8 range through a solid band of 5.10 to 5.12, with a couple at 5.13, so there is something for both intermediate and strong climbers. The sandstone is gritty, can be fragile, and should not be climbed on after rain.
al_turtle_rock.parking_note: Drive up County Road 70 to the lot at the top of the ridge in the county park.

al_grotto.blurb: The Grotto is a compact sandstone section of Sand Rock, also known as Cherokee Rock Village, a county park near Leesburg above Weiss Lake. It offers a mix: about ten sport routes, a few trad lines, and several boulder problems from easy to fairly hard. Roped grades stretch from the 5.8 range up into the 5.13s and one 5.14, so it works for intermediates and strong climbers alike. It is best known for a short, burly roof crack. As elsewhere in the park, the sandstone is gritty and should be left alone after rain.
al_grotto.parking_note: Drive up County Road 70 to the lot at the top of the ridge in the county park.

al_harvest_wall.blurb: Harvest Wall is a traditional wall at Jamestown, a long sandstone escarpment in northeast Alabama owned in part by the Southeastern Climbers Coalition. All 21 routes are trad, ranging from easy 5.6 and 5.7 climbs through a good supply of 5.9 to 5.10 lines, and topping out with a few 5.11s. Several lines are long, so bring a generous rope. The cliff seeps and can stay wet for a week or more after rain.

al_blevins_gap.blurb: Blevins Gap is a bouldering area inside Blevins Gap Nature Preserve, a Land Trust of North Alabama property in south Huntsville. The boulders cluster around the Sugar Tree trailhead and hold 21 problems, from easy warm-ups to a few very hard lines, with most in the middle grades. The trail to the boulders was still being built at last report, so expect rough going.
al_blevins_gap.parking_note: Use the Sugar Tree trailhead for the nearby boulders, and do not block driveways. Other boulders are reached from the main lot off Cecil Ashburn Drive. Trails are open dawn to dusk.
